strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored computer-vision problem: general-purpose representation learning from high-resolution 3D medical images under limited paired image–text data. Treating this as an Algorithms/General contribution is appropriate.

The empirical study is broad and unusually informative. It examines report augmentation, field of view, patch size, pooling, batch size, contrastive loss, report generation, and masked-image modeling, followed by evaluation on retrieval, classification, report generation, and segmentation.

The strongest results are meaningful: COLIPRI-C improves CT-RATE classification probing over Merlin by about 2.6 AUPRC and 1.5 AUROC points and also leads on the external RAD-ChestCT dataset. For report generation, COLIPRI variants improve RadBERT Macro-F1 by roughly 17–19 points and positive-finding RadFact F1 by 6–9 points over the evaluated encoder baselines.

Evaluation includes an external classification dataset and three segmentation datasets, rather than relying exclusively on the pretraining distribution. Report-generation results include bootstrap confidence intervals and clinically oriented metrics in addition to lexical overlap.

The paper is clear and candid about negative results: MAE remains substantially better for segmentation, short-prompt zero-shot performance is brittle, and adding RRG or MAE can reduce global classification quality. The appendix supplies substantial preprocessing, probing, and prompt detail.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the principal ingredients—CLIP, CapPa-style report prediction, and MAE—are established, and their combination does not demonstrate the advertised synergy. The final COLIPRI-CRM model is not the strongest variant on classification, zero-shot classification, report generation, retrieval, or segmentation; simpler COLIPRI-C, -CR, or -CM variants generally win. Thus, the evidence supports a useful empirical recipe family more strongly than a unified comprehensive objective.

The “native zero-shot” protocol averages embeddings from 50 labeled positive and 50 labeled negative target-domain reports per abnormality. This uses class-labeled examples to construct prototypes and is materially different from ordinary language-prompt zero-shot classification. Comparisons to baselines are also imperfect because their prompting protocols are unavailable and fVLM excludes two classes. The strongest zero-shot claims should therefore be qualified.

The key retrieval gains are presented in development/validation tables after extensive tuning, but no final held-out retrieval comparison appears in the main results. This weakens a central claim and raises selection-overfitting concerns.

Reliability evidence is limited relative to the extensive hyperparameter search: pretraining results lack multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates, segmentation uses only three of five folds and contains acknowledged anomalously low runs, and statistical significance is not assessed for classification or segmentation. The reported small differences among several variants may therefore be noise.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully secure. The reproduced CT-CLIP probe is dramatically below published performance and is attributed to a possible configuration issue, while the report-generation comparison covers only a small set of encoder baselines rather than establishing state of the art against specialized report-generation systems. Consequently, the broad state-of-the-art wording is stronger than the evidence.

Reproducibility has gaps despite the detailed appendix: there is no clear code/checkpoint release statement, sampling ratios for alternating CT-RATE and NLST training are insufficiently specified, adapted GPT-based RadFact prompts and few-shot examples are not supplied, and the claimed learning-rate reduction “by a factor of 2 to 3×10^-5” is inconsistent with the earlier 6×10^-4/3×10^-4 settings.

For a clinically motivated system, evaluation remains limited to aggregate metrics. There is no subgroup, scanner/site, calibration, or failure-mode analysis, and no discussion of risks from hallucinated reports or deployment beyond acknowledging low absolute report accuracy and domain shift. These omissions constrain the clinical-impact claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult computer-vision problem: learning reusable representations from high-dimensional 3D CT volumes with limited paired reports. The evaluation is unusually broad, covering retrieval, classification, zero-shot transfer, report generation, and three segmentation datasets.

The manuscript provides useful empirical observations about 3D vision-language training, including the benefit of small 3D patches, the trade-off between field of view and resolution, and the severe sensitivity of zero-shot performance to prompt style. The authors also report important negative results rather than hiding them.

Report-generation transfer is the most convincing result. Under a common frozen-encoder/Qwen setup, COLIPRI substantially improves RadBERT Macro-F1 and positive-finding RadFact-CT scores over CT-CLIP, CT-FM, and Merlin. The paper appropriately notes that absolute factual performance nevertheless remains low.

The methodology and preprocessing are described in considerable detail, including model schedules, report transformations, downstream protocols, and the GPT prompts used for report restructuring. External evaluation on RAD-ChestCT is also valuable.
weaknesses: The algorithmic originality is limited. COLIPRI largely transfers established CLIP, CapPa-style report generation, and MAE objectives to 3D CT, followed by an extensive hyperparameter search. More importantly, the proposed combination does not demonstrate the promised synergy: RRG and MAE generally reduce classification performance, the final CRM model is not the strongest model on the principal tasks, and every COLIPRI variant is substantially worse than plain MAE pre-training for segmentation.

The reported “native zero-shot” protocol is not conventional zero-shot classification: each class prototype is formed by averaging 50 reports selected using positive or negative abnormality labels. This introduces class-labeled examples into the classifier construction, and the manuscript does not clearly state the split from which those reports are sampled. Comparing these label-conditioned prototypes against published baselines using different prompts—and, for fVLM, a different 16-label subset—does not support a clean state-of-the-art zero-shot claim. The ordinary short-prompt results are much weaker.

The claimed classification probing result is confounded by the evaluation procedure. The method called a “linear probe” searches over five aggregation heads and four learning rates, although several aggregation heads contain newly trained attention blocks and are explicitly non-linear. This tests a larger trainable readout and model-selection budget rather than linear separability. The very large discrepancy for CT-CLIP relative to published results further indicates unresolved implementation or configuration problems.

The evidence does not isolate the value of the proposed objectives from architecture, data, preprocessing, report rewriting, and evaluation choices. A controlled Primus-M baseline trained on the same paired data with a standard CLIP recipe is shown mainly during development, while the headline comparisons use models with different architectures and pre-training corpora. The report-generation gains likewise cannot establish that RRG caused the improvement because COLIPRI-CM—not the RRG-specific model—is best on most clinical metrics.

Statistical support is inadequate for the breadth of the hyperparameter search. Most pre-training ablations appear to be single runs, no seed variation or uncertainty is reported for classification and zero-shot results, and validation performance is repeatedly used to select many architectural and augmentation choices. The segmentation table flags several runs as “unexpectedly low” without diagnosing instability, yet provides neither repeated seeds nor significance analysis.

The adapted GPT-4o-based RadFact-CT metric is not validated against radiologist judgments, while the strongest clinical claims rely heavily on it. Even the best positive-finding Logical F1 is only 20.4, so the generated reports remain far from clinically reliable. Claims about supporting clinical decisions should therefore be more restrained, accompanied by expert evaluation, calibration and safety analysis.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed prose: the manuscript does not provide a code or checkpoint release commitment, random seeds, total compute for the full sweep, the exact sampling source for native prototypes, or enough information to reproduce confidence intervals. Overall, the work contains useful engineering observations and promising report-generation results, but the weak novelty, evaluation confounds, and failure of the central multi-objective combination to deliver consistent gains make the current acceptance case unconvincing.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: learning general-purpose 3D medical vision-language representations from limited paired data while exploiting additional image-only CT data.

Provides a broad, well-organized empirical study spanning retrieval, linear probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, and segmentation. The extensive design ablations on report augmentation, field of view, patch size, pooling, batch size, and auxiliary objectives offer useful practical guidance for the community.

Demonstrates convincing gains on global tasks. COLIPRI-C improves classification probing over strong public encoders on both CT-RATE and the external RAD-ChestCT dataset, while the COLIPRI variants substantially improve clinically oriented report-generation metrics, including roughly 17 points in RadBERT Macro-F1 and 7 points in positive-finding RadFact F1 over the best reported baseline.

The evaluation is unusually candid: it reports absolute report-generation performance as still low, exposes substantial prompt sensitivity, and clearly shows that MAE remains considerably better for segmentation. These negative results make the conclusions more credible.

The manuscript is generally clear and supplies substantial implementation detail, preprocessing prompts, downstream training settings, confidence intervals for report generation, and comparisons under a common probing/report-generation pipeline. weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the methodological originality is moderate: report generation, CLIP-style alignment, and MAE are established objectives, and the primary contribution is their careful adaptation and combination for 3D CT rather than a fundamentally new method.

The auxiliary objectives do not establish the intended comprehensive synergy. COLIPRI-C is best for classification, COLIPRI-CM is best for report generation, MAE is clearly best for segmentation, and the full COLIPRI-CRM model is not consistently best. In particular, the report-generation objective itself does not convincingly improve downstream report generation beyond MAE, with overlapping confidence intervals.

The “native zero-shot” protocol is closer to labeled prototype construction than conventional zero-shot classification because each class representation averages 50 reports selected using positive/negative abnormality labels. The source split and sampling procedure for these reports should be explicit. Comparisons are also imperfect because baseline results use different prompts and, for fVLM, only 16 of the 18 abnormalities.

Most development ablations appear to be single runs from sequential star sweeps, without variance estimates or confirmation of interactions among selected choices. Classification results lack uncertainty, and segmentation uses only three of five folds, includes conspicuously weak runs, and provides no statistical analysis.

The dense-task evidence remains weak for the paper's general-purpose framing: COLIPRI provides little or no improvement on lung segmentation and trails matched MAE pre-training substantially. The acknowledged preprocessing mismatch between pre-training and segmentation further complicates interpretation.

Generalization is evaluated only within chest CT and closely related anatomy. Dependence on proprietary GPT-4o preprocessing, limited information about releasing the processed reports/code/checkpoints, low absolute factual report-generation scores, and the absence of clinician evaluation or a fuller clinical-risk discussion limit reproducibility and near-term clinical significance.

strengths: This is a technically ambitious and unusually comprehensive Algorithms/General submission. It combines contrastive image-report alignment, report generation, masked image modeling, and the proposed Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) in a coherent 3D vision-language pre-training framework.

The empirical scope is strong: the encoders are evaluated on classification probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, bidirectional retrieval, and four segmentation datasets. Evaluation includes an external classification dataset (RAD-ChestCT), five-fold segmentation experiments, confidence intervals for major classification and report-generation results, and both short and long fine-tuning schedules.

The results are compelling on global and multimodal tasks. COLIPRI-CM/CRM substantially improve classification, zero-shot classification, retrieval, and clinically oriented report-generation metrics over the evaluated public encoders. Generalization gains on RAD-ChestCT are particularly valuable.

OSL addresses a practically important mismatch between long training reports and short, polarity-sensitive inference prompts. The ablation shows a large improvement for short-form prompting while largely preserving native-prompt performance.

Using unpaired NLST scans through the MAE objective is well motivated by the scarcity of paired 3D medical data. The results convincingly show that MAE supervision is important for retaining dense-task utility while also improving several global tasks.

The appendix provides extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, prompts, preprocessing choices, and component ablations. The authors also acknowledge clinically low absolute report-generation accuracy, the remaining zero-shot/probe gap, and the limited benefit of the RRG objective.
weaknesses: The central OSL construction assumes that a finding absent from a report subsection is absent from the image. Radiology reports are incomplete and omit incidental or clinically irrelevant findings, so sampled counterfactuals can be false negatives. Likewise, the mechanical template “No {sentence}” can produce linguistically or clinically awkward negations. The paper does not quantify this label noise through expert review or compare against higher-quality negation generation.

The claimed benefit of jointly combining all objectives is less decisive than the headline results suggest. COLIPRI-CM is often comparable to or better than COLIPRI-CRM, while the RRG objective has minimal or negative effects on several metrics and does not improve downstream report generation. Much of the dense-task performance comes from MAE initialization: without it, COLIPRI-CM performs near COLIPRI-C. A clearer factorial comparison against the same MAE-initialized model without continued MAE or language training would better isolate the contribution of multimodal joint training.

Several state-of-the-art comparisons are not fully controlled. Some zero-shot baseline numbers are imported from another paper; CT-CLIP performs anomalously poorly under the authors’ probing setup; and retrieval comparison is primarily against a reported CT-CLIP result. Differences in preprocessing, crops, prompts, model capacity, and evaluation implementation therefore complicate the broad “SOTA across all standard tasks” claim.

The so-called linear probing protocol searches over 20 configurations and includes trainable attention-pooling modules, some with multiple learned queries. This is a reasonable frozen-backbone evaluation but is not strictly linear probing and provides more adaptation capacity than the terminology implies.

Segmentation improvements over the matched MAE baseline are modest and inconsistent relative to fold variability. Under long training, COLIPRI-CRM improves only slightly over MAE and remains below ResEnc-L on LiTS and KiTS23 while underperforming simpler references on some other datasets. No repeated-seed uncertainty or statistical test is supplied for these small differences.

Report-generation gains rely heavily on RadBERT trained in the CT-RATE ecosystem and GPT-4o-based RadFact evaluation. Although complementary lexical and clinical metrics are reported, expert clinical evaluation is absent, and the positive-finding RadFact F1 remains only about 22%. Thus the results support better representation quality, not readiness for clinical report generation.

The OSL probability in Eq. 5 appears malformed: the temperature is placed outside one exponential term in the denominator. This is likely a typographical error, but the implemented formulation should be stated unambiguously.

Reproducibility is otherwise strong, but training variance, random seeds, total compute, and the exact public release location are not provided in the manuscript. The medical setting would also benefit from dataset-demographic analysis and a more explicit discussion of bias, privacy, and deployment risks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored computer-vision problem: learning versatile representations from high-resolution 3D CT volumes using both paired reports and substantially more abundant image-only data.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering zero-shot and probe-based classification, report generation, bidirectional retrieval, and four segmentation datasets. The external RAD-ChestCT classification evaluation is particularly useful.

COLIPRI-CM/CRM deliver substantial gains over the reported 3D baselines on classification, retrieval, and positive-finding report metrics. The improvements are not limited to a single benchmark or metric.

The Opposite Sentence Loss is a simple, practically motivated approach to the mismatch between long training reports and short, polarity-sensitive inference prompts. Table 3 shows a large improvement for short-prompt zero-shot classification.

The paper contains extensive implementation details, prompts, preprocessing descriptions, component variants, confidence intervals, and per-fold segmentation results. It also candidly reports that report-generation supervision provides little downstream benefit and that absolute clinical report quality remains low.
Combining multimodal learning with MAE initialization is empirically useful: Tables 1, 2, 5, and D.5 show that it produces representations effective for both global and dense tasks.
weaknesses: The main scientific gains are not cleanly attributable to the proposed contributions. The strongest results come from COLIPRI-CM/CRM, while Table D.5 shows that prior MAE initialization is essential and Table B.7 shows almost no improvement from adding RRG to CM. There is no sufficiently controlled decomposition of MAE initialization, continued MAE training, additional NLST data, CLIP, OSL, and RRG under matched compute.

Baseline comparisons are not adequately controlled for architecture, spatial resolution, data volume, parameter count, or compute. Some headline zero-shot numbers are copied from another paper, whereas the authors' own CT-CLIP implementation performs dramatically below its reported result and is attributed to an unresolved 'potential configuration issue.' This weakens the state-of-the-art claims.

The proposed OSL rests on a questionable label assumption: if a report subsection contains no positive finding, the paper treats a pathology sampled from another report as absent and its negation as correct. Radiology reports are not exhaustive, so an unmentioned condition is not necessarily absent. No audit quantifies this label noise, GPT-4o preprocessing errors, or the grammatical and semantic validity of template negations.

The evidence for OSL is incomplete. The central with/without-OSL comparison in Table 3 is only on the CT-RATE validation set, uses one final configuration, and reports no uncertainty or repeated training runs. A test-set and external-dataset ablation, including per-condition results and comparisons to simpler prompt/negation augmentation, is needed.

The claimed 'classification probing' is not consistently linear: several candidates contain learned attention-pooling modules, and the best of 20 probe configurations is selected. This is a reasonable downstream protocol, but it does not support claims about linear separability and can obscure differences in intrinsic representation quality.

Uncertainty estimates bootstrap test examples but do not capture variation from pre-training or downstream training. Most ablations appear to be single runs, and marking all confidence-interval overlaps as best is not a substitute for a paired statistical comparison.

Report generation is evaluated without expert review, largely using a CT-RATE-trained classifier and GPT-4o-based factuality judging after GPT-4o was also used to restructure the training reports. These metrics may reflect dataset/style compatibility, and the best positive-finding RadFact F1 remains only about 22%. Claims of clinically relevant semantics and clinical support should therefore be tempered.

Generalization is limited. Report generation and retrieval are evaluated only on CT-RATE, while the sole external evaluation covers classification. RAD-ChestCT is still chest CT, and the segmentation datasets are deliberately selected from nearby anatomical regions. Robustness across institutions, acquisition protocols, demographic groups, and non-chest anatomy is not demonstrated.

The conclusion overstates the evidence by claiming state-of-the-art performance across all standard tasks. In Table 5, COLIPRI does not consistently beat the MAE baseline and remains below ResEnc-L on several segmentation datasets; RRG adds negligible or negative effects to several metrics.

There are reproducibility concerns despite the detailed appendix: the manuscript's model/code link is blank, NLST access is controlled, GPT-4o preprocessing introduces cost and version dependence, and the processed reports or a manual quality assessment are not documented as being released. Equation 5 also appears malformed relative to the stated temperature-scaled softmax.

strengths: This is a strong and unusually comprehensive study of 3D medical vision-language pretraining. COLIPRI combines contrastive image-report alignment, the proposed Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL), report generation, and masked image modeling in a coherent framework, with extensive implementation and preprocessing details. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/3690b6585c6942c88d28c6c03599af9a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The OSL addresses a practical and clinically relevant problem: the mismatch between long training reports and short, polarity-sensitive diagnostic prompts. The targeted ablation is convincing: removing OSL reduces short-prompt CT-RATE AUROC from 81.66 to 74.09, while native-prompt performance changes much less.

The empirical scope is excellent. Evaluation covers linear probing, zero-shot classification, bidirectional retrieval, report generation, and four segmentation datasets. COLIPRI-CM/CRM consistently improve global-task performance, including external evaluation on RAD-ChestCT; report-to-image R@5 rises from 2.9 for CT-CLIP to 35.1 for COLIPRI-CRM, and report-generation clinical metrics improve substantially over all evaluated baselines.

The study includes unusually extensive ablations of report augmentation, field of view, patch size, pooling, losses, batch size, report-generation design, and MAE configuration. Confidence intervals are reported for the major classification and report-generation comparisons, and five-fold results are supplied for segmentation.

The paper is clear, well organized, and appropriately candid about important limitations: generated reports remain far below clinical requirements, the report-generation pretraining objective has little downstream effect, zero-shot performance still trails probing, and the transformer does not consistently outperform strong CNN segmentation systems.
weaknesses: The central performance gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the novel OSL or report-generation objective. Much of the improvement comes from MAE initialization and continued MAE training: Table D.5 shows large degradation without MAE initialization, while the RRG objective provides only small or inconsistent benefits and does not improve downstream report generation. Thus, the final system's novelty is more modest than its broad state-of-the-art framing suggests.

OSL supervision relies on a potentially unsafe assumption: if a report subsection contains no positive finding, a finding sampled from another report is treated as absent. Radiology reports are incomplete and omission does not reliably establish absence, so this construction can introduce systematic false negatives. A noise analysis, radiologist validation of sampled pairs, or comparison with labels would strengthen the technical case.

Baseline comparability is imperfect. Models differ substantially in architecture, pretraining data, resolution, and input handling; the authors' CT-CLIP evaluation is dramatically below published results; and 2D baselines are reduced through ad hoc slice averaging or pooling. Several headline comparisons also use values copied from another paper without common confidence intervals. These results demonstrate a strong system but do not always isolate methodological superiority under controlled compute and data.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance 'across all standard tasks' is overstated. On segmentation, COLIPRI mainly matches or slightly improves the authors' MAE baseline and remains below ResEnc-L on several datasets; on Lung, training from scratch is better under long fine-tuning. Report generation has strong relative gains but low absolute positive-finding F1, and retrieval is evaluated only in-distribution on CT-RATE.

External generalization remains limited to another chest-CT dataset and the same small abnormality vocabulary. Retrieval and report generation lack external-institution evaluation, subgroup analysis, and robustness testing across scanners, populations, contrast protocols, or report styles. These omissions matter for the clinical-generalization implications, though the paper appropriately avoids claiming deployment readiness.

There are minor technical and presentation issues: Eq. (5) appears to misplace the temperature outside one denominator exponential; segmentation results lack uncertainty or statistical testing across folds; many ablation choices appear selected from single runs on the same validation suite; and the promised public model/code links are blank in the anonymized manuscript, preventing present verification of reproducibility.
